title: Delhi High Court Orders Takedown of Vulgar Content Exploiting PhysicsWallah Founder's Identity
excerpt: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani grants interim injunction protecting Alakh Pandey's personality rights, directing Google, Meta, X, and Telegram to remove sexually explicit and impersonation content.
body:
• The Delhi High Court ordered the takedown of online content found to be vulgar, commercially exploitative, or impersonating PhysicsWallah founder Alakh Pandey, in an interim order passed by Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani.
  • The suit names Google, Meta, X, and Telegram as intermediaries, with the court directing them to furnish basic subscriber information of offending accounts.
  • Pandey alleged widespread misuse of his name, image, and catchphrase 'hello bachho' through sexually explicit stickers, impersonation pages, and coupon-code scams.
  • One YouTube video referring to Pandey as 'scamwala' was excluded from the injunction and will be considered separately.

The Delhi High Court has ordered the removal of online content that commercially exploits, impersonates, or produces sexually explicit material using the name and likeness of Alakh Pandey, the founder of edtech unicorn PhysicsWallah, according to LiveLaw and MediaNama.

Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani passed the interim order after issuing summons in Pandey's personality rights suit, marking the latest in a growing line of Delhi High Court rulings that extend personality-rights protections to public figures in the digital age.

Three Categories of Abuse

The court examined a tabulated summary of allegedly infringing URLs submitted by Pandey's counsel, categorising the material into three groups: vulgar or sexually explicit content, material that commercially exploits Pandey's personality, and content that impersonates him.

Pandey's suit alleged that his name, image, and signature catchphrase "hello bachho" — familiar to millions of Indian students — had been misused across platforms. The alleged violations ranged from sexually explicit stickers and GIFs featuring his likeness to impersonation pages and coupon-code scams falsely claiming association with him.

The suit names several intermediaries, including Google, Meta, X, and Telegram, alongside unidentified defendants. The court directed these platforms to take down the identified content and furnish the basic subscriber information sought by Pandey's legal team.

The 'Scamwala' Exception

In a notable distinction, Justice Bhambhani excluded one YouTube video referring to Pandey as "scamwala" from the interim injunction. The video, which had received approximately 50,000 views, will be considered separately at a later hearing.

Pandey's counsel clarified that the objection was limited to this specific video and not to two other critical videos that remain available on the platform. The argument was framed not as an attempt to suppress criticism or humour, but to challenge the specific allegation that Pandey was a "scamster."

"Let's remove it, then let the aggrieved party come."

— Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani, on a disputed URL

During the hearing, Telegram objected to one URL allegedly promoting a "PW Lectures" channel, arguing that evidence of commercial activity at the URL was not included in the plaint. The court directed the link to be removed regardless, with Justice Bhambhani observing that the aggrieved party could challenge the order later.

A Growing Legal Frontier

The ruling extends a line of personality-rights cases in Indian courts that have expanded rapidly in recent years. The Delhi High Court has previously granted similar protections to actors including Amitabh Bachchan, Anil Kapoor, Abhishek Bachchan, Ravi Kishan, and Salman Khan, often in response to AI-generated content and deepfakes.

PhysicsWallah itself is no stranger to the courtroom. In January 2026, Justice Jyoti Singh granted a separate injunction restraining a former employee from publishing defamatory content and using deceptively similar marks such as "Scam Wallah" and "Emotion Wallah." That ruling held that freedom of speech does not protect defamatory, malicious, or abusive speech calculated to injure reputation.

PhysicsWallah Limited, which began as Pandey's YouTube channel in 2014, has grown into a publicly listed edtech unicorn. The company operates more than 207 YouTube channels with approximately 98.8 million subscribers, serves over 3.5 million registered students, and runs 303 Vidyapeeth offline coaching centres across India.

Implications for Creators and Platforms

For the Indian creator economy, the ruling reinforces that personality rights extend beyond traditional celebrities to digital-first figures who have built substantial public followings. The order's directive to platforms to disclose subscriber data raises questions about the balance between user privacy and the enforcement of personality-rights claims.

For diaspora audiences, the case underscores the evolving intersection of digital identity protection and Indian law — particularly relevant as Indian-origin content creators build global followings and face cross-border misuse of their likenesses.

What's Next

The matter has been listed for further hearing, with the "scamwala" video and broader questions around the scope of Pandey's personality-rights claims still to be resolved. The outcome could set further precedent for how Indian courts treat online criticism versus exploitation of public figures.
